title: The cost of discipleship
hookLine: Dietrich Bonhoeffer warns against cheap grace, grace without discipleship
last: JESUS CHRIST IS THE ONE WORD.

cards: Clearance sale. Everything must go. Grace, forgiveness, comfort, all marked down to nothing, no questions asked.

That's roughly the picture a young German pastor painted of his own church. Dietrich Bonhoeffer was a Lutheran, from a church built on the teaching that God's grace is free, a gift nobody can earn. He held to that.
And still he said the church had started giving grace away the wrong way, like stock it was trying to clear. He had a name for it.

teach.b: Bonhoeffer was teaching young pastors for the Confessing Church, the church that said no at Barmen, in a small seminary the government would later close. Out of that teaching came a book.
In English it's The Cost of Discipleship. In German its title is one word, Nachfolge, following after. It opens with two kinds of grace.

teach.h: CHEAP GRACE: GRACE WE HAND OURSELVES.
teach.b: Cheap grace, he wrote, is grace we hand ourselves: forgiveness without turning around, church membership without following, grace without the cross, without Jesus, a doctrine we nod at and then live exactly as before.
Costly grace is the other kind. He reached for Jesus's short parable in Matthew.

In the King James Bible: "the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field."
Notice the joy. The man isn't paying a fine. He's found something worth everything.
That's costly grace: still a gift, never earned, but a gift that calls you to follow.

teach.h: IT COSTS A LIFE, IT GIVES A LIFE.
teach.b: Bonhoeffer put it in a pair of phrases people still repeat: it is costly because it costs a life, and it is grace because it gives a life.

Jesus said something close in Luke: "For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost?" Christians have argued about the book ever since. Some hear a needed alarm.
Others worry it leans too hard on effort and forgets the comfort of grace. He later said he could see dangers in it, though he stood by it. What makes it hard to brush off is what he did next.
He kept following, right into the danger.

how: The Cost of Discipleship is read in church study groups and seminaries across denominations, often alongside the Sermon on the Mount, which takes up much of the book.

games.q: the cost of discipleship — tap the pairs.
p: sells all he has, for joy

s: Bonhoeffer taught that grace must be earned
he taught grace is a gift. his warning was against grace that asks nothing and changes nothing.
the German title of the book means following after
in the parable, the man sells everything grudgingly
"for joy thereof" he sells all he has. costly grace still comes with joy.

games.q: you're a Lutheran pastor. your church preaches that grace is free. what do you warn against?
o: grace handed out with no call to follow.
games.why: Bonhoeffer kept grace free, and warned against cheap grace: forgiveness without turning around, grace without the cross.

practice: There's probably one good thing you know you should do and keep putting off because it will cost you something: an apology that admits you were wrong, a long call, giving something you'd rather keep.
Don't decide anything; just look honestly at the cost, and whether there's a field with treasure behind it. If you pray, bring it to God.

wordCard.voice: Bonhoeffer. The German pastor who wrote The Cost of Discipleship, warning against cheap grace that asks nothing and changes nothing.

orig.note: Greek: to follow, the verb in Jesus's call to Matthew, follow me (Matthew 9:9).

carryVoice: Your line: not cheap grace. Still a gift, but one that calls you to follow. See you tomorrow.
